articles.title: EPA considers further narrowing Clean Water Act protections
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Friday said it will consider further narrowing protections for streams and wetlands under the Clean Water Act. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and Army Corps of Engineers issued a supplemental proposed rule that they said would be likely to reduce the bodies of water that are under the Clean Water Act’s…
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Friday said it will consider further narrowing protections for streams and wetlands under the Clean Water Act.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and Army Corps of Engineers issued a supplemental proposed rule that they said would be likely to reduce the bodies of water that are under the Clean Water Act’s jurisdiction if its changes are adopted.

It would be expected to reduce the number of waters subject to the Clean Water Act in the West.

That means development or pollution in these streams and wetlands would no longer require a permit or potential mitigation.

The new changes come on top of an already proposed rule by the agencies that is also expected to narrow the Clean Water Act’s applicability. The additional proposal could narrow it further.

The EPA said in a press release that it is considering the new proposal “alongside” the rule it proposed last year as part of an effort to evaluate a wider range of options as it determines its final approach for regulating streams and wetlands.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said in a written statement that the agency is aiming to set up a “durable” rule that “follows the law and ends burdensome regulatory uncertainty.”

“Today’s action reflects our continued commitment to transparency and public input, ensuring we have fully considered a wide range of potential policy options. We look forward to public feedback on this supplemental notice, which will help strengthen the real-world expertise behind the final rule,” he said.

However, environmental advocates raised concerns about the potential changes, saying they could worsen health and safety outcomes.

“This is a very big deal. It puts a lot of pressure on states to protect waters; it’s going to result in higher treatment costs. It’s going to result in waters that … ourselves and our kids …. swim and fish in to be less safe and more polluted,” said Jim Murphy, the National Wildlife Federation’s associate vice president for legal advocacy.

“It’s going to result in higher drinking water costs, higher health risks. It’s a step backwards in terms of public health and safety,” Murphy added.

The rule in question concerns which waters are considered “Waters of the United States” and therefore subject to Clean Water Act protections.

In 2023, the Supreme Court narrowed the definition to only waters that are “relatively permanent, standing or continuously flowing.” It said that wetlands need to have a “continuous surface connection” with a protected body of water.

But questions remained about how to define those terms.

In its supplemental proposal, the Trump administration suggested defining “relatively permanent” streams as those that have standing or flowing water every day for at least 11 months out of the year.

Similarly, it proposed to define a protected wetland as one that has standing or flowing surface water that is continuously connected with surface water in another body that is already regulated by the clean water act every day for 11 months of the year.

articles.title: PG&E (PCG) Sub Says California’s Wildfire Bill Leaves Financing Risk Unresolved. What Protection Is Still Missing?
articles.summary: Pacific Gas and Electric Company, the regulated utility subsidiary of PG&E Corporation (NYSE:PCG), said California Senate Bill 492 would improve wildfire-sur...
articles.body:
Pacific Gas and Electric Company, the regulated utility subsidiary of PG&E Corporation (NYSE: PCG ), said California Senate Bill 492 would improve wildfire-survivor recovery and strengthen preparedness, but would not resolve the financing risk created by the state's wildfire-liability framework. The amended bill would establish a fast-pay claims program, would expand statewide preparedness planning, and would adjust financing mechanics for the Wildfire Fund's Continuation Account.

California's inverse-condemnation framework can make utilities responsible for property damage from utility-caused wildfires regardless of negligence. Although the Wildfire Fund can reimburse eligible claims, a state-commissioned study concluded that existing funding mechanisms are insufficient and presented options for a more durable system. Senate Bill 492 would not fully adopt those structural reforms.

The proposed California Wildfire Relief Fast-Pay Program would create standardized procedures for reviewing claims, making settlement offers, and paying approved amounts. A faster alternative could reduce litigation costs, shorten recovery, and improve cost visibility.

The amended bill would require a statewide community wildfire preparedness strategy, county-level planning support, improved risk-data standards and more detailed annual reporting. Better coordination and clearer data could direct mitigation spending toward the communities facing the greatest exposure.

The amended bill would also impose safety-linked executive-compensation requirements following qualifying catastrophic fires and authorize the Wildfire Fund Administrator to incur debt and issue bonds supporting the Continuation Account. For PG&E Corporation (NYSE:PCG), those measures could make wildfire response more predictable while reinforcing incentives to reduce ignition risk.

The central financing problem would remain if Senate Bill 492 became law in its current form. The Wildfire Fund protects participating utilities only to the extent that sufficient resources are available for eligible claims. A severe event, or several large events, could consume available capacity and expose PG&E Corporation (NYSE:PCG) to a substantial funding requirement while claims, reimbursements and regulatory recovery remain unresolved.

The state study outlined broader options, including a more durable fund with diversified funding sources, external risk transfer, liability reform and state-administered wildfire-liability insurance for electric utilities. Other options included a state backstop for utility wildfire liability and a separate state-backed catastrophe-reinsurance layer for residential property insurance. Senate Bill 492 would improve the existing framework but would not establish a comprehensive replacement or a clearly sufficient backstop for extreme losses.

articles.title: Trump administration moves to fast-track oil drilling approvals in Alaska
articles.summary: The Trump administration announced on Friday that it was proposing to fast track approvals for oil drilling projects in Alaska after a request from a trade group to do so. The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) issued a proposal that would seek to quickly approve oil and gas drilling in the National Petroleum Reserve in…
articles.body:
The Trump administration announced on Friday that it was proposing to fast track approvals for oil drilling projects in Alaska after a request from a trade group to do so.

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) issued a proposal that would seek to quickly approve oil and gas drilling in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska (NPRA).

In 1923, then-President Warren G. Harding set aside the reserve as an emergency oil supply for the Navy. Since that time, drilling projects have been approved there , but environmental advocates have also raised concerns about impacts to wildlife .

In its proposal, the BLM said it would consolidate multiple approval procedures into a single review and set timelines that it hopes will “expedite” project approvals.

It said that the agency would have to approve some rights-of-way or drilling permit applications within 60 days.

It said that its move came in response to a petition from the Alaska Oil and Gas Association, a trade group representing oil and gas companies operating in the state.

That petition called for a “uniform and efficient process to approve production projects similar to those that have already been approved” in the reserve. The trade group’s request also included the 60-day approval timeline.

“Responsible development shouldn’t be held back by redundant paperwork,” BLM director Steve Pearce in a written statement.

“This is about working smarter, honoring the Trump administration’s commitment to energy security, and ensuring Alaskans directly benefit from the resources in their backyard,” he added.

articles.title: Microsoft says virtually nobody was grabbing NYT articles through its chatbot
articles.summary: Microsoft claimed in a legal filing that its Copilot chatbot hardly ever regurgitates sentences from articles and books used to ground the AI.
articles.body: Microsoft’s Copilot rarely reproduces even full sentences from news articles and books, let alone substantive chunks that could substitute for the original, the company says in new legal filings as it fights copyright claims from publishers including The New York Times and book authors. As part of the lawsuit’s discovery, Microsoft provided 8.2 million Copilot chat logs to an expert hired by news publishers. The logs, it claims, were specifically chosen “because they hit on keywords implicating use of News Plaintiffs’ websites, and therefore the most likely to contain News Plaintiffs’ works.” It says the resulting analysis shows that 59,545 of these contained at least 16 words in common with news content used to ground the AI model. An expert for the Center for Investigative Reporting found 51 instances of “substantial overlap” with CIR work in the dataset, Microsoft says. Similarly, an expert in the authors’ suit found that the 8.2 million conversations with Copilot only had 24 responses that contained at least 30 matching words. Only 10 of the 212 books evaluated had any matches, Microsoft claims. The Times, CIR, and Authors Guild did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Microsoft argues that the numbers bolster its case that using copyrighted content for AI training datasets should be considered fair use. While systems like Copilot rely on using copyrighted material, it says, the resulting systems are used for significantly different purposes than the original. The fact that they sometimes reproduce sections of text, it concludes, “hardly undermines the transformative purpose of LLM training.” The filings were made as part of a legal battle brought by publishers and authors against Microsoft and OpenAI, which the plaintiffs claim built products on their works and now compete with them directly, in part by regurgitating copyrighted content. The news publishers’ and books authors’ claims were consolidated under one judge to streamline the process, despite objections from the publishers and authors. Microsoft submitted its filing on Friday as it argues for the judge to issue a summary judgement, which would end the case at an early stage. (The Trump administration also filed a statement of interest in the New York Times case this week, supporting OpenAI.) If the judge sides with the publishers and authors, the legal battle will continue in court.

articles.title: Fake patient portal scam can steal your login and infect your PC
articles.summary: MyChart phishing emails mimic real patient portal alerts with fake lab results and malware tricks that target Windows users across the country.
articles.body: If you have ever checked a lab result or sent your doctor a message online, you may already know MyChart. It is a widely used patient portal from Epic that hospitals and medical practices use to give patients online access to health information and care teams. That growing reliance on patient portals caught the attention of Mary M. She recently wrote to us after hearing from her primary care physician, or PCP, and several specialists about moving more of their patient communication online. "I just got a lot of updates from my PCP and specialist doctors saying they are moving toward this, but they are already compromised!! I think this is a topic for you!" Mary raised a concern many patients may share as they hear about scams targeting MyChart users. There is an important point to clear up. The warnings reviewed here describe criminals impersonating MyChart through phishing campaigns. They do not report a breach of the MyChart platform itself. MEDICARE AND SOCIAL SECURITY SCAMS: WARNING SIGNS AND TIPS Epic has documented scams that copy the MyChart experience to steal login details. One version can also push malware onto Windows computers. Here's how the scam works and how to protect yourself before a fake MyChart alert catches you off guard. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com Why the MyChart phishing scam is getting attention now This one caught my attention because the warnings are coming from several credible sources at nearly the same time. Penn Medicine said on Aug. 26, 2026, that it was seeing a nationwide scam involving emails and text messages made to look like they came from MyChart. Then, on Aug. 28, Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday warned consumers about another MyChart impersonation scam involving a bogus Medicare Kit. Epic has also detailed two phishing campaigns its security team investigated this summer. Put all of that together, and you can see why I want you to be especially careful with unexpected MyChart messages right now. The tricky part is that many of us are already used to getting legitimate emails about appointments or new test results. A fake MyChart alert can land right alongside the real ones, and scammers are counting on you reacting before you take a closer look. How the fake MyChart results scam works One campaign starts with a message that looks routine. Epic says the email carries MyChart branding and tells the recipient, "Your recent results are ready." The button inside the email leads to a fake sign-in page. According to Epic, scammers copied code from the real MyChart site, which helps the page look convincing. The bogus page asks for an email address and password. If you enter them, the scammers can capture those credentials. Then the attack gets more aggressive. Fake medical results create panic After the victim signs in, the fake site displays a made-up medical record. Epic says one version shows a pop-up claiming an "AI-powered review" found critical patterns in blood work. That is a powerful pressure tactic. A warning about your health can be much harder to ignore than an ordinary phishing message. Epic says real critical results come from your care team rather than a website pop-up. The fake chart then claims you need to complete a human verification step before seeing more information. The verification step can install malware This part should stop you immediately. Epic says the site instructs Windows users to press the Windows key and R, paste content from the clipboard and press Enter. Those steps open the Windows Run box and execute a command the website placed on the clipboard. According to Epic, following those instructions installs malware. Epic also saw an August 2026 version with an "Unlock Full Report & See Diagnosis" button. Clicking it downloaded a Windows file called Full_Analysis_Report.exe. The page then coached the victim through bypassing the computer's security warning. Your medical results should appear inside MyChart. A patient portal should never require you to download a Windows program to reveal a diagnosis. FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK Another scam promises a free Medicare Health Kit The second campaign uses a different hook. Epic says scammers sent fake emails telling people they had been selected for a "2026 Medicare Health Kit." Penn Medicine has also warned about messages advertising a free "MyChart Medicare Kit" or "Senior Health Package." MyChart does not run giveaways. After someone clicks, Epic says the link can pass through unrelated advertising sites before reaching a fake MyChart-branded survey. A countdown clock pushes the victim to move quickly. Eventually, the site says the kit costs $0 but asks for a shipping fee. Before payment, it collects personal information. The final page asks for credit card details. Epic says no kit ships. Why a fake MyChart message can be so convincing Patients already expect electronic messages from doctors and hospitals. A real test-result notification may show up on the same day as a fake one. Scammers can copy that familiar routine. They can also use fear to shorten the amount of time you spend checking a message. If a fake portal hints at a serious health problem, your first instinct may be to find out what happened. That is why opening the portal independently can make such a difference. We recently covered another healthcare scam that uses fake QR codes around medical settings. Those codes can send patients to bogus sites asking for patient portal credentials or Medicare information. The MyChart campaign follows the same basic idea. The scammer borrows trust from a healthcare service you already recognize. How to stay safe from fake MyChart messages A few simple steps can help you slow things down before an urgent-looking message leads you to the wrong place. 1) Open MyChart yourself If an email says a new result is waiting, avoid using the button inside the message. Open the MyChart app directly. You can also use a saved bookmark or start from your healthcare provider's official website. Epic says each healthcare organization can have its own MyChart URL. You can use MyChart.org to find your provider's official portal. 2) Check the full sender address Do not rely on the sender name alone. An email can display "MyChart" while coming from an unrelated address. Look at the full address and compare it with previous legitimate messages from your healthcare provider. If anything feels off, contact your provider through a phone number or website you already trust. 3) Never run computer commands for a patient portal MyChart says it will never tell you to use keyboard shortcuts or run a command to verify, fix or unlock your account. A website asking you to open the Windows Run box should be an immediate warning sign. Close the page. 4) Use two-step verification MyChart supports two-step verification (2FA). The extra check can help protect your account if someone gets your password. Depending on your setup, you can verify your login through a code or an authenticator app. MyChart also supports passkeys, which can reduce your reliance on a reusable password. 5) Give MyChart its own password Avoid reusing a password from another important account. A password manager can create and store a strong password for you. If a phishing site captures one password, reuse can turn one stolen login into a much larger problem. 6) Keep security protection running The malware part of this scam shows why strong security protection still has a role. Strong antivirus software can help warn you about malicious downloads or suspicious websites. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com. Keep Windows and your browser updated too. For more ways to recognize suspicious email, see our guide on how to spot and prevent phishing attacks in your inbox. 7) Verify scary medical claims another way If a message claims a serious result needs immediate attention, do not let the urgency decide what you click. Open the official MyChart app yourself or call your provider using a number you already trust. Epic specifically warns that real critical results come from your care team rather than a scary website pop-up. 8) Reduce the personal information scammers can find about you Scammers can make phishing messages more convincing when they already know details such as your phone number, home address, age or family connections. A data removal service can help remove some of that information from people-search sites and data brokers. It will not stop a fake MyChart message from reaching you, but it can give scammers less personal information to work with when they try to make a message feel legitimate. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. 9) Treat MyChart giveaways as a red flag Epic says MyChart does not run giveaways. If an email promises a free Medicare kit or health package under the MyChart name, do not enter personal information or payment details. FAKE PARTY INVITATION SCAM CAN HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER What to do if you already clicked a fake MyChart link Your next move depends on what happened after you opened the page. If you clicked but entered nothing Close the page. If you did not enter any information, run a command or download a file, avoid interacting with the site any further. Mark the original message as junk or phishing. Do not click an unsubscribe link inside the suspicious message. If you entered your MyChart password Go to MyChart through the official app or your provider's trusted website. Change your password right away. Then review the contact information saved in your account, including your email address and phone number. If anything looks unfamiliar, contact your healthcare organization's MyChart help desk. If you entered credit card information Call your bank or card issuer using the number printed on the card. Tell them the card information went to a fraudulent website and ask about replacing the card. If you ran the Windows command or downloaded the program Disconnect the computer from the internet. Have the computer checked before you use it again for sensitive activity. Run a full security scan with strong antivirus software. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. Then change important passwords from another trusted device if you used those accounts on the affected computer. If your medical information looks wrong Contact your healthcare provider and health insurer. Medical identity theft can create problems beyond a stolen password. Fraudulent activity can end up connected to your health records or insurance. We explain the warning signs and recovery steps in medical identity theft follows you into the doctor's office. Kurt's key takeaways What gets me about this scam is how naturally it fits into something many of us already do. Doctors want patients using portals because they make it easier to see results and stay connected with a care team. Scammers know those messages already have our attention. I would keep using MyChart if my doctors rely on it. I would simply change how I respond to unexpected notifications. If an email says an important result is waiting, I would open the app myself rather than letting the email choose where I go. The malware trick also deserves extra attention. A website asking you to open the Windows Run box or ignore a security warning has crossed a very clear line. Close it and verify the message through your provider. The hardest part may be resisting the fear factor. A message about an abnormal medical result can make anyone move quickly. Taking a few extra seconds to open the real app could protect your patient account and your computer. articles.title: Fed’s Hammack Says It’s Time to Act to Bring Down Inflation
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack said it’s time for the US central bank to act to cool inflation.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack said it's time for the US central bank to act to cool inflation.

"Right now, what I'm hearing is that it's time to act," Hammack said Friday in a LinkedIn post.

Hammack, one of three policymakers to dissent from the Fed's decision to hold interest rates steady in July, said both data and anecdotes from her district are telling her that monetary policy is not sufficiently weighing on the economy right now.

In her post she described a conversation with a manufacturer in Northeast Ohio who told her the Fed should raise interest rates because he's seeing double-digit inflation in many of his input prices.

Policymakers next meet Sept. 15-16 to vote on interest rates. They enter a communications blackout period at midnight. Investors put the odds of a rate increase at this month's meeting at slightly above 60% after a surprisingly strong jobs report on Friday.

articles.title: Nearly a third of AI chatbot replies to voting questions inaccurate, outdated: Study
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence chatbots are becoming a source for voters to ask questions about upcoming elections, but a new study determined nearly a third of AI-generated replies could be inaccurate or outdated. In a report released Thursday, researchers with the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) tested 15 different generic prompts across six AI chatbots and found…
articles.body:
Artificial intelligence chatbots are becoming a source for voters to ask questions about upcoming elections, but a new study determined nearly a third of AI-generated replies could be inaccurate or outdated.

In a report released Thursday , researchers with the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) tested 15 different generic prompts across six AI chatbots and found 29 percent of responses were incomplete, inaccurate or outdated. Generic questions included topics like mail-in voting, voter registration and important dates.

Errors included misidentifying Election Day dates and showing outdated requirements and deadlines, according to the report.

In 16 percent of the replies, the chatbot answered correctly but did not include important information that could be useful to a voter, such as key deadlines or ways to prove identity.

The models tested were Meta’s Muse Spark, xAI’s Grok 4.3, DeepSeek’s V4 Pro, OpenAI’s GPT-5.5, Anthropic’s Sonnet 4.6 and Google’s Gemini 3.5 Flash.

The ISD, which focuses on extremism, disinformation and online threats, tailored the prompts to 10 states with a history of electoral process changes, related legislation or election administration controversy.

“As LLMs [large language models] play a larger role in shaping the information environment, the reliability and behavior of these systems will increasingly affect voter access and trust,” ISD researchers wrote. “This analysis finds that models’ overall accuracy on election process is mixed, and concerns remain over a reliance on outdated sources, overconfidence in relaying nuanced and conditional information, and performance divergences between languages.”

OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 was deemed the most accurate model, answering 89 percent of the responses with specific, complete and correct information. Gemini 3.5 Flash came in second, answering 84 percent of questions accurately, while Grok 4.3 fell behind at 66 percent, Sonnet 4.6 at 64 percent, DeepSeek at 63 percent and Muse Spark at 61 percent.

Researchers said all of the models also returned some outdated information, though DeepSeek — made by a Chinese AI startup — showed the most outdated information, such as referencing 2024 election dates.

The accuracy drastically plummeted 16 percentage points when prompted in Spanish, researchers noted. Answers in Spanish were also more likely to be outdated or inaccurate, with every model’s performance dropping for the language.

When researchers tested for “adversarial claims,” all six models refuted false or misleading claims at high rates when asked in English, though the rates were mostly similar in Spanish as well. Muse Spark and Gemini had the most ambiguous or hedging responses, at 22 percent and 18 percent, respectively.

Despite concerns over accuracy, researchers said many of their findings are “encouraging,” as the large language models largely cited authoritative sources for answers and “effectively confront[ed]” false claims at high rates.

Except for Meta, researchers tested the models through their application programming interfaces, which are made for developers and can differ from the consumer-facing software most of the public uses.

A spokesperson for Google’s Gemini pointed to this when reached for comment, stating the consumer version of the model “has different protections and is how most people use our AI.” They also pointed to the disclaimer shown on the Gemini app, which states, “Election info changes quickly. Verify responses with official sources.”

“Gemini is designed to respond with accurate and timely information and performed well in this analysis,” the spokesperson added.

For Meta, analysts used “clean research accounts without links to existing Meta accounts,” according to the report.

When asked about the report, OpenAI maintained its focus on securing AI systems ahead of elections.

“As elections take place around the world, we are committed to continuing to elevate accurate voting information, combat misuse by bad actors, and increase transparency,” the spokesperson said.

DeepSeek, xAI, Meta and Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

Researchers laid out a series of recommendations to counter concerns with AI models. They urged election officials and civil society organizations to treat official websites as a direct input into these models and update them frequently.

They also asked model developers to reduce a models’ overconfidence when responding to conditional or ongoing election questions and to “close the language gap.”

articles.title: WNBA commissioner stepping down after this season
articles.summary: Englebert has presided over expansion, but has been criticized for the league’s handling of Caitlin Clark and trans policies.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert is retiring at the end of the year, following seven years in the role.

NBA Commissioner Adam Silver announced the news Friday.

“Cathy has presided over the WNBA through the most significant period of growth in the league’s 30-year history,” Silver wrote in a statement. “We are grateful for Cathy’s leadership and unwavering commitment to the advancement of women’s basketball.”

With Engelbert at the helm, the WNBA expanded from 12 teams to 18 by the end of 2030. Transformative media rights and collective bargaining agreements also led to increases in salaries and benefits for athletes.

“In 2019, I had the privilege of being appointed the league’s first commissioner and to lead a league with enormous potential yet untapped awareness and significant undervaluation,” Englebert said. “Over the years, it has been amazing to watch WNBA players thrive and lead the massive cultural surge around women’s sports.”

However, the commissioner was also criticized by players for her lack of connection to the league and her leadership style.

Recently, she said the league would continue to have discussions regarding transgender athletes , an issue which has become a major one for Republican lawmakers. She called it a complex and nuanced issue, saying in a memo that the league would continue discussions on the topic.

That memo came after two former NBA players, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, declared themselves to be eligible for the WNBA draft because they identified as women.

Engelbert also took criticism for the number of hard fouls Caitlyn Clark, a prodigious player and among the most popular female athletes on the planet, has taken in her first three seasons in the league.

The outgoing commissioner is expected to lead a succession plan and has submitted a list of candidates to take over the role for consideration.

articles.title: Epinephrine injection recalled over potentially fatal health risks
articles.summary: Consumers, retailers and health care facilities should stop using the product and discard or return it, the FDA said.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A pharmaceutical company is voluntarily recalling three lots of epinephrine injections, USP 30 mg/30 mL, over sterility concerns and the potential presence of particulate matter.

American Regent initiated the nationwide recall after customers complained about “leaking and cracked vials,” according to a company notice posted by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration . “The firm’s investigation also revealed the presence of particulate matter identified as Nylon, Cellulosic, Acrylic, Polyethylene and Glass,” the company said.

The company said epinephrine injections are used to treat allergic reactions and to increase blood pressure in adults, warning that intravenous administration of the medication “containing particulate matter may lead to serious adverse health consequences.”

Particulate matter can cause life-threatening blood clots, permanent organ damage or death, the FDA explained. Cracked vials can jeopardize sterility, potentially contaminating the medication and posing another health risk for patients.

American Regent is notifying distributors and customers by mail. Consumers, retailers and health care facilities should stop using the product and discard or return it.

The company has so far received no reports of adverse events related to the recall.

Anyone with questions can contact American Regent at 1-800-645-1706, Monday through Friday during standard business hours.

articles.title: The White House is making arcade games racist
articles.summary: Tetris isn’t happy about it.
articles.body: The PR masterminds at the White House just released a series of vaguely policy-themed “arcade” games, some of which are racist — and modeled on real games whose copyright holders may not be too happy to be associated with the MAGA agenda. The Tetris Company has already responded to “Build the Wall,” which is obviously modeled on the famous puzzle game. In the Trump administration’s game, the player has to stack interlocking shapes to stop a “zombie border siege” along the southern border. Aliens — the administration’s preferred term for noncitizens, and the subject of previous grotesque attempts at humor — run across the screen, trying to get to America before the gates are shut. In a statement to The Verge, Tetris spokesperson Kerri Brusca clarified that the company wasn’t involved in the creation of Donald Trump’s game. “For more than 40 years, Tetris has brought people together across generations and cultures through play and joy. The objective of the game has always been to stack with purpose to clear as many lines as possible,” Brusca said. “We are currently reviewing the matter.” The various companies whose brands the White House ripped off to make and promote these games — including Sega, Nintendo, Xbox, and the Flappy Bird Foundation Group — did not immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment. Previously, the Trump administration has gotten in trouble for infringing on others’ copyrights. The Department of Homeland Security has had to delete some of its racist, fancam-esque posts after receiving DMCA takedown requests. The purpose of Trump’s interminable memes, games, and other gimmicks is manifold: to drum up support for Trump’s policies, to entertain his groyper fans, and, of course, to troll the libs. (One game, “Rio Run,” is like snake, except the head of the snake is a Border Patrol agent who collects migrants as he moves across the screen. Ha ha, get it? The president is deporting people.) But the games also inadvertently highlight the administration’s policy failures, not to mention the hypocrisy of Trump’s agenda. Trump’s efforts to build a wall through protected lands in the Southwest, including Big Bend National Park, has been met with mass opposition — even from Republicans in deep-red Texas who form a key part of the MAGA coalition. Other games are similar reminders of how Trump’s policies are backfiring, even on the right. There’s “Flappy Bill,” a play on Flappy Bird that involves getting a bald eagle to deliver a piece of legislation to the National Mall. Cute! Except the administration has rolled back protections under the Endangered Species Act, the landmark legislation that helped rescue bald eagles from the brink of extinction. The administration’s supposed revamping of the National Mall has also been unpopular. In “Supply Line,” reminiscent of the game Tapper, you have to knock processed foods — those filled with additives, seed oils, and artificial colorings — off a conveyor belt before they get fed to schoolchildren. But Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. hasn’t managed to do any of that. Besides issuing a likely AI-drafted report for his Make America Healthy Again commission, RFK Jr.’s main role at HHS has been to roll back vaccine recommendations and food safety regulations. The administration’s gutting of the Food and Drug Administration made it harder to investigate the spread of cyclosporiasis, the so-called explosive diarrhea parasite, earlier this year. If anything, these games serve as a great reminder that our well-being is a big joke to the president and the people who surround him.

articles.title: Trump says data center opponents face ‘poverty, crime and squalor’
articles.summary: President Trump took aim at data center opponents again Friday, suggesting they want to “go through poverty, crime and squalor.” It marks the second time this week that Trump has gone after critics of AI infrastructure, which has become increasingly unpopular among Americans in recent months. “If you want to get rich as a state…
articles.body:
President Trump took aim at data center opponents again Friday, suggesting they want to “go through poverty, crime and squalor.”

It marks the second time this week that Trump has gone after critics of AI infrastructure, which has become increasingly unpopular among Americans in recent months.

“If you want to get rich as a state or as a town, if you want to pay lower taxes, if you want to create tremendous wealth, if you want your house to be more valuable and everything else, you’re going to want a data center,” Trump said after an unrelated signing in the Oval Office.

“If you want to go through poverty, crime and squalor, I would say don’t approve data centers,” he continued. “You know, you have your choice. So I’m all for people approving them or not.”

The president similarly suggested in a Truth Social post on Monday that the “only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.”

He has long embraced the push to build more data centers across the country, an endeavor that tech companies argue is necessary to support AI development.

But Americans have grown wary of such projects over concerns they could result in higher electricity costs, strain water resources and produce noise or air pollution.

While data centers have brought in greater tax revenue for some communities, numerous jurisdictions used tax breaks to attract the investments. States including Ohio and Illinois have paused such tax incentive programs in recent months, while others have moved even more aggressively, with New York instituting the nation’s first statewide freeze on new “hyperscale” data centers.

Trump’s comments come as Democrats and Republicans alike have sought to distance themselves from the server warehouses powering the AI boom, which are increasingly becoming a central issue in the midterm elections.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D), who once touted new Amazon data centers in the Keystone State, announced new restrictions on development last month, as he faced attacks on the issue from his Republican opponent.

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for Senate in Michigan, has called for a one-year moratorium on new data center projects, and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) paused data center construction pending state audits.

articles.title: Lancaster County, PA infant confirmed to have died from measles
articles.summary: A six-week-old infant’s death in Pennsylvania was caused by measles, the Lancaster County coroner confirmed Friday. County coroner Stephen Diamantoni said the child, who died last month, was born with Amish lethal microcephaly, a rare genetic condition that can cause respiratory infections. Pennsylvania health officials last week announced the “measles-related” deaths of two unvaccinated people,…
articles.body:
A six-week-old infant’s death in Pennsylvania was caused by measles, the Lancaster County coroner confirmed Friday.

County coroner Stephen Diamantoni said the child, who died last month, was born with Amish lethal microcephaly, a rare genetic condition that can cause respiratory infections.

Pennsylvania health officials last week announced the “measles-related” deaths of two unvaccinated people, including an infant, as the state grapples with an outbreak that has sickened 577 people and hospitalized 98 as of Friday.

Their deaths were the first measles-related deaths in the state in 35 years and the first in the U.S. this year.

It has not been confirmed if the six-week-old child was one of the previously-announced two cases.

At the time, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention did not confirm whether measles was the cause of death in both cases.

“Available information does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths or whether the individuals died from other causes while infected with measles,” the CDC’s website read. “CDC will update the national count as additional information becomes available.”

Diamantoni said in an interview with Lancaster Online, which first reported details of the child’s death, that his office began to investigate the second case after the announcement from state health officials.

After learning of the child’s Amish lethal microcephaly diagnosis and reviewing her medical records, he said he was able to confirm that the cause of death was measles.

According to Diamantoni, the clinic that was treating the child did not initially report the case to the coroner because the child’s death was not surprising. Children diagnosed with that genetic condition often die within months of birth from viral respiratory illnesses.

“The child did test positive for measles. We know that children with this disorder will die of respiratory infections,” Diamantoni said. “Measles is a respiratory infection and we know the life expectancy of these poor kids is very short.”

Trump administration officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., have questioned Pennsylvania’s handling of the measles outbreak, publicly feuding with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) over transparency.

“We don’t know exactly what happened in Pennsylvania yet,” Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said in an interview with Fox Business.

“We don’t know if the children died from measles or had another condition that was already attacking them and they happened to get measles at the same time.”

articles.standfirst: Segundo a Nova Rota do Oeste, motorista da carreta não se feriu e recusou encaminhamento médico.
articles.summary: Segundo a Nova Rota do Oeste, motorista da carreta não se feriu e recusou encaminhamento médico.
articles.body:
Uma carga de carne foi saqueada por pessoas que passavam pela BR-163 após uma carreta tombar no km 747 da rodovia, em Sorriso (MT), nessa sexta-feira (4). Segundo a concessionária Nova Rota do Oeste, responsável pelo trecho, o motorista não se feriu .

A concessionária informou que o acidente envolveu uma carreta, com placa de Londrina (PR) , carregada com carne. Com o tombamento, a carga ficou espalhada e foi saqueada após outros motoristas que passavam pelo local estacionarem os veículos para levar a carne (assista acima) .

Uma equipe de resgate da Nova Rota do Oeste foi até o trecho e avaliou o motorista. Ele saiu ileso e assinou um termo recusando o encaminhamento para atendimento médico.

Após o acidente, um poste de iluminação pública também caiu sobre a faixa de domínio da rodovia .

Levar mercadorias de um veículo envolvido em acidente sem autorização do proprietário pode configurar crime de furto , previsto no artigo 155 do Código Penal , com pena de um a quatro anos de prisão, além de multa . A carga continua tendo proprietário mesmo quando fica espalhada pela rodovia ou quando se trata de produto perecível.

Além disso, quem compra, recebe ou transporta produtos saqueados sabendo da origem ilícita pode responder por receptação, prevista no artigo 180 do Código Penal. A pena para o crime pode chegar a quatro anos de prisão.

A concessionária não informou o que provocou o tombamento nem a quantidade de carne que era transportada ou saqueada.

articles.body:
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon spokesman and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s top choice for the next Army secretary, is among at least four candidates being considered for the role, sources familiar with the process told The Hill this week.

The field also includes at least two current officials — Marc Anderson, an assistant secretary of the Army, and Derrick Anderson, an assistant secretary of Defense — and Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.), an Army veteran who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee, sources said.

Former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll’s departure from the Trump administration this week closed the book on an 18-month tenure in which the close ally of Vice President Vance pushed for rapid modernization of America’s largest fighting force, but repeatedly clashed behind-the-scenes with Hegseth.

That leaves the Army without a Senate-confirmed leader on the civilian or uniformed side of operations, after Hegseth in April forced out the Army’s widely respected chief of staff, Gen. Randy George.

On Thursday, President Trump announced that Adam Telle , the current assistant secretary of the Army for Civil Works, would be the Army’s acting secretary, catching some current and defense officials by surprise.

Telle, an Alabama native, has spent years working in Republican offices on Capitol Hill, most recently as Sen. Bill Hagerty’s (R-Tenn.) chief of staff.

“My previous work in the Army focused on moving at Trump Speed to deliver on one of the Army’s original missions. I will apply that same relentless focus on efficiency to how the Army mans, trains, equips, and modernizes,” Telle said in his first statement as acting Army Secretary on Friday.

It is unclear when Trump will nominate a permanent replacement for Driscoll, or whether Telle might be tapped to stay in the role for the long-term.

Multiple sources inside and outside the Pentagon said Hegseth’s choice would be Parnell, who is also his senior advisor.

“Every senior leader in [the] Pentagon knows that Secretary Hegseth’s preferred pick is Sean Parnell,” a senior Pentagon official said. “Sean’s well-respected across the Department, and viewed as a solid choice.”

The Hill first reported last week that Hegseth was considering choosing Parnell for the post once Driscoll departs the administration.

Parnell has support from multiple senior White House officials and some of the president’s outside advisers, according to four sources with knowledge of the matter.

Parnell has been in touch with the White House about the role in recent days, one Pentagon official said this week. But a senior administration official denied it, adding that Parnell is “100 percent focused on executing the job he has now.”

When reached for comment on Friday, the White House referred The Hill to Trump’s Thursday Truth Social post announcing Telle as acting Army secretary.

White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles is leading the search for Driscoll’s replacement, sources told CBS News .

Parnell, who was awarded two Bronze Stars and a Purple Heart for his service in Afghanistan, ran for Congress twice. With Trump’s endorsement, he ran for Senate in Pennsylvania, but withdrew from the race in November 2021, losing a court fight over custody of his three children, which included faced allegations of abuse by his enstranged wide. Parnell has denied the allegations. Parnell said in 2024 he had been “vindicated” and he now shares custody of all five of his children, Pentagon officials said.

A senior government official with close knowledge of the situation told The Hill that there is “eagerness” among “most” of the Army’s three- and four-star generals to work with Parnell “given his institutional and combat experience.”

Some officials have argued that Parnell could have a tough time being confirmed and his possible selection has already drawn rebuttals from some defense-focused Democrats.

“Sean Parnell is Liar-in-Chief for this disastrous war in Iran. Now, Pete Hegseth wants to reward him by making him SecArmy,” Rep. Pat Ryan (D-N.Y.), a West Point graduate who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, said on Thursday. “He’s dangerously unfit for the job and we must stop him.”

Another person floated by some in the administration is Mast, who served for 12 years in the Army and has earned multiple medals, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

However, plucking Mast from the House would further degrade the GOP’s slim majority in the lower chamber. Mast, who currently holds a safe red seat in Florida, recently met with Hegseth, according to an administration official.

Some within the administration fear Mast’s vocal support for Israel could rankle the MAGA base.

“Mast has already pitched himself to everyone in DC who will listen, including Secretary Hegseth; he’s a try-hard and largely viewed as out of touch with Trump supporters,” the official said.

Mast’s office did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Derrick Anderson, a former GOP congressional candidate in Virginia who is currently Assistant Secretary of Defense for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict, is another name in the mix, according to two people familiar with the discussions.

Marc Anderson, the assistant Secretary of the Army, Financial Management and Comptroller, is also being mentioned as the potential successor to Driscoll, one person familiar with the discussions within the Pentagon said.

Marc Anderson, who has held multiple executive leadership roles within venture capital, is not well known outside of Army circles.

NBC News reported on Friday that Sam Brown, the undersecretary for memorial affairs at the Department of Veterans Affairs, is being floated by some in Congress and in the administration as a possible Driscoll replacement. He ran unsuccessfully twice for Senate in Nevada.

Brown, a West Point graduate, deployed to Afghanistan as part of Operation Enduring Freedom in Kandahar, eventually medically retiring with the rank of captain.

"I can't stand high taxes," Smith said (1). "And if y'all think I'm lying, federal income tax is nearly 40% for people in my range. And then, on top of it all, is an additional 13.6% in the state of California. And we ain't even getting the L.A. city tax. And we ain't getting FICA, Social Security and disability."

And his criticism goes beyond the Golden State.

"It's similar in New York. I got a problem with that. So, because of that, I speak out against liberal policies that come to take your money," he added.

"I'm looking for another crib in Florida. So, in about two months from now I might be in Florida. I got to have primary residence. I'm getting murdered in taxes in New York and LA. Come on, man, that's too much. I'm in the two highest tax states," Smith complained (4).

articles.body:
U.S. Central Command (Centcom) on Saturday conducted strikes on several Iranian crude oil carriers in response to “multiple unprovoked” Iranian attacks on two U.S. Navy warships, according to the military command.

The U.S. military “permanently disabled” three of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’s (IRGC) crude oil carriers located near Kharg Island and in the Gulf of Oman. No U.S. service members were harmed during the Iranian attacks, according to Centcom.

“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours,” Centcom Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement shared on social media. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”

The exchange of hostilities follows escalating military operations from both sides this week. After the U.S. carried out roughly 100 strikes against Iranian targets on Tuesday, Tehran responded by targeting U.S. military bases and allies in strikes across the Middle East.

Vice President JD Vance waived off concerns about the state of the conflict during a Thursday press briefing, telling reporters he “wouldn’t call it a war.”

“Right now, there is no active shooting,” he continued. “I recognize there have been places where this has flared up.”

President Trump and his administration have repeatedly pushed back on public criticism of this conflict, which has now stretched into a sixth month. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has placed a strain on the global energy supply, raising fuel and other costs for U.S. consumers.

“A lot of people don’t call it a war. I call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us. It’s not a big thing,” the president told reporters in the Oval Office on Friday.

articles.summary: Some of the U.S. military’s highest-ranking officials were subject to polygraph tests as part of a sweeping Pentagon investigation into leaks to journalists on dwindling weapons stockpiles amid the Iran war, multiple reports suggest. Military officials and civilian employees were tested in August, including roughly 50 members of the Joint Staff, according to the New…
articles.body:
Some of the U.S. military’s highest-ranking officials were subject to polygraph tests as part of a sweeping Pentagon investigation into leaks to journalists on dwindling weapons stockpiles amid the Iran war, multiple reports suggest.

Military officials and civilian employees were tested in August, including roughly 50 members of the Joint Staff, according to the New York Times — which first reported the investigation Friday.

Several dozen other officials, including U.S. Central Command and other combatant commands , were also tested earlier this summer, CBS News reported.

Investigators reportedly questioned officials on whether they had disclosed classified information surrounding munitions shortages , including long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors, to members of the press.

No one failed the questions, aimed to weed out anyone who may have leaked this information, two officials told CBS, adding that Joint Chiefs Chair Gen. Dan Caine was not among those tested.

President Trump was furious over the disclosures, according to CBS, which reported that only a small number of people had access to the classified information. One official said investigators were also concerned about the possibility someone with high-level access could be working with foreign intelligence.

Polygraph exams are commonly conducted on officials with access to highly classified information. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security similarly used the devices to determine the source of press leaks.

But in this case, current and former officials reportedly describe the number of senior military personnel tested in the investigation as extraordinary.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell told CBS the department “takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly.”

The investigation follows months of reporting about the rate at which the U.S. has used some of its most advanced weapons since the war with Iran began on Feb. 28.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has pushed back on reports of shortages, while President Trump publicly laid out his anger over leaks within the department.

“The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down,” the president wrote in an August Truth Social post. “Long term jail sentences will be sought!”
